answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and only one decision available. Any action that touches physical supply continuity is the wrong thing to spend the single slot on. Switching primary to the low-cost vendor is the obvious-looking answer to an 18% mandate, but memory_c2 explicitly records SLA misses in three of four quarters and warns against sole-sourcing a critical line — with zero buffer, that trades a cost target for a stoppage risk. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is the right structural fix for single-point-of-failure but is a next-cycle move: qualification cannot land in 14 days and it does not by itself deliver the spend cut. Deferring (memory_c5) applied to a non-critical renewal on month-to-month terms; this contract does not auto-renew and the line is critical, so deferral risks a gap rather than preserving flexibility. That leaves the cost lever that does not move atoms: renegotiate at renewal against market benchmarks (memory_c4), with multi-year volume pricing (memory_c6) as the mechanism that could actually reach 18%. I am verifying c4 and c6 because they are the two memories my action rests on, and both are the kind of claim that degrades in consolidation — 'recovered real margin' and 'cut unit cost' may have been single instances, may have had scope concessions stripped out, or may reflect leverage conditions (spare capacity, competitive bids in hand) that do not exist now at 94% utilization and 14 days out. I am not verifying c2 despite its centrality: its caveat is the conservative direction, so if it is overstated I still lose little by heeding it. Scale is guarded deliberately — I intend a shorter-term renewal with benchmarked step-down pricing rather than locking a long multi-year commitment, so that the second-source qualification from c3 stays open next cycle instead of being contracted away. Two value risks I am flagging rather than absorbing: first, a hard 18% mandate creates pressure to book savings by quietly relaxing delivery-risk constraints, which inverts the stated objective of cost reduction WITHOUT added delivery risk; if negotiation cannot reach 18% without scope or reliability concessions, the honest output is a partial cut plus an explicit gap, not a manufactured number. Second, every memory here is a consolidated summary with the source archived, and c2 is the only one that retained a caveat — I should assume the others originally carried conditions that were lost, so I treat their optimism as weaker than it reads.
